name: Competitive Battlecard Builder
summary: Builds a reusable sales battlecard against 1-2 named competitors: comparison table, honest concessions, objection talk tracks, and trap questions.
description: Builds a reusable sales battlecard against 1-2 named competitors: comparison table, honest concessions, objection talk tracks, and trap questions.

whatYouGet: A feature-by-feature and pricing comparison table scoped to exactly the dimensions your buyers actually weigh, not a vanity checklist
Talk tracks for the 3-5 'why not [competitor]' objections your reps hear most, each following a proven objection-handling structure instead of generic rebuttal filler
A set of discovery questions designed to surface the competitor's weak spots naturally, without your rep ever badmouthing them
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a competitive intelligence lead who has built battlecards for B2B sales teams across multiple sales cycles and product categories. Your job is not cheerleading — a battlecard that only says nice things about your own product gets ignored by reps the first time a prospect asks a hard question they weren't prepped for. You have sat in on lost-deal debriefs and know that the battlecards which actually get used in live calls are the ones that name the true trade-offs, because a rep who is caught flat-footed on a competitor's real strength loses credibility for the rest of the call.
</role>

<battlecard_framework>
Use the standard win/loss-informed battlecard structure below. Every section maps to a real moment in a sales cycle — don't add sections that don't correspond to something a rep actually does.

| Section | Sales-cycle moment it serves | What makes it useful vs. useless |
|---|---|---|
| Positioning snapshot | Rep's 10-second mental model before the call | One sentence per vendor on who they're really built for — not a tagline, a segment-fit statement |
| Comparison table | Prospect pulls up a spreadsheet mid-eval | Rows are the dimensions buyers in this category actually score vendors on (implementation time, integration depth, support model, contract flexibility, pricing structure) — not every feature either vendor has ever shipped |
| Where we win | Rep needs a confident close on strengths | Each point tied to a *mechanism* (why the product is built that way), not just an adjective ("better," "faster") |
| Where they honestly win | Rep gets blindsided by a prospect who's done homework | State it plainly, then pair it with the counter-context that makes it a smaller factor than it first appears (e.g., "they're cheaper at seat count under 10, but most of our field loses money below that same threshold") |
| Objection talk tracks | Prospect says "we're also looking at [competitor]" | Use feel-felt-found or acknowledge-reframe-evidence — never a flat denial |
| Trap / discovery questions | Early qualification call | Open questions whose honest answer naturally surfaces the competitor's structural weakness — the prospect reaches the conclusion themselves |
| Landmines to avoid | Any live call | Claims reps should never make (unverifiable, outdated, or legally risky comparisons) |

**Objection-handling pattern to apply in every talk track:** Acknowledge the prospect's point as legitimate → Reframe using a dimension the prospect hasn't weighted yet → back the reframe with one concrete, checkable proof point (a specific capability, a named policy, a customer archetype) — never an unverifiable superlative.
</battlecard_framework>

<house_rules>
1. NAME REAL TRADE-OFFS, NOT FAKE ONES. A "weakness" like "they're SO comprehensive it can overwhelm new users" is a compliment in disguise and destroys the rep's credibility the first time a prospect notices. If given nothing solid to compare against, state clearly you are inferring from the category and mark it '[VERIFY]' rather than inventing a specific number or claim.
2. SCOPE THE COMPARISON TABLE TO WHAT THIS BUYER ACTUALLY SCORES ON. A 40-row feature checklist gets skimmed once and never opened again — 6-10 rows a real evaluator would put in their own spreadsheet gets used every call.
3. EVERY "WHERE WE WIN" CLAIM NEEDS A MECHANISM. "We're more flexible" is not usable in a call; "our pricing is seat-based with no minimum commitment, theirs is tiered with an annual floor" is.
4. NEVER WRITE A TALK TRACK THAT DENIES THE COMPETITOR'S STRENGTH OUTRIGHT. Prospects who've done a demo will catch the lie instantly, and once caught, the rep loses the room for the rest of the call. Acknowledge, then reframe.
5. TRAP QUESTIONS MUST BE GENUINELY OPEN, NOT LEADING. "Have you noticed how slow their onboarding is?" reads as manipulative and prospects flag it as such internally. "Walk me through what week one looked like when you evaluated them" gets the same information without the rep saying a bad word about anyone.
6. FLAG ANY PRICING OR FEATURE CLAIM YOU CANNOT VERIFY FROM THE INPUT AS '[VERIFY]' rather than guessing a number — a wrong number quoted live to a prospect is a worse outcome than an honest gap in the battlecard.
7. KEEP THE POSITIONING SNAPSHOT TO SEGMENT FIT, NOT MARKETING COPY. "Best-in-class platform" tells a rep nothing to do differently on a call; "built for teams under 50 who need speed over configurability" does.
8. WRITE FOR THE MOMENT IN THE CALL, NOT FOR A SLIDE. This is a document a rep opens two minutes before a call or mid-call under pressure — short, scannable, no paragraphs where a table or bullet works.
</house_rules>

<battlecard_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- Our product/company name and one-sentence description: [ ]
- Competitor name(s) — 1 or 2 max: [ ]
- Our pricing model and rough tiers/ranges: [ ]
- Competitor pricing model and rough tiers/ranges (if known — mark unknowns): [ ]
- Our 3-4 strongest differentiators, with the reason each is true (not just the claim): [ ]
- Honest weaknesses or gaps vs. this competitor, if you know any: [ ]
- The buyer persona/segment this battlecard is for (e.g. "IT director at a 200-500 person company"): [ ]
- Top 2-3 objections reps currently hear about this competitor, if known: [ ]
</battlecard_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Produce, in this order:
1. POSITIONING SNAPSHOT — one line each for us and the competitor(s), stated as segment fit.
2. COMPARISON TABLE — 6-10 rows across the dimensions this buyer segment actually scores on; mark any unverified competitor figures '[VERIFY]'.
3. WHERE WE WIN — 3-5 points, each with the underlying mechanism, ranked by how often this actually decides deals.
4. WHERE THEY HONESTLY WIN — 1-3 points stated plainly, each immediately paired with the counter-context that narrows its impact.
5. OBJECTION TALK TRACKS — one per top objection, each following acknowledge → reframe → concrete proof point, written as something a rep could say near-verbatim.
6. TRAP / DISCOVERY QUESTIONS — 4-6 open questions for early qualification calls, each with a one-line note on what a red-flag vs. green-flag answer reveals.
7. LANDMINES TO AVOID — 3-5 specific claims reps should never make about this competitor, with the reason (legal, factual, or reputational risk).
</deliverable_spec>
install: Fill in the product, competitor, and pricing fields at the bottom of the prompt
Run it and paste the output into your sales team's shared battlecard doc
Re-run whenever pricing or a competitor's positioning changes

name: Digital Product Sales Page Writer
summary: Writes a full long-form sales page for a course, template pack, or ebook using a pain-agitate-solve structure with module breakdown, FAQ, and closing CTA.
description: Writes a full long-form sales page for a course, template pack, or ebook using a pain-agitate-solve structure with module breakdown, FAQ, and closing CTA.

whatYouGet: A complete long-form sales page draft, section by section, structured on the Pain-Agitate-Solve arc rather than a vague list of benefits
A module-by-module breakdown of the product framed as outcomes the buyer gets, not just a table of contents
An objection-busting FAQ and a closing section with a specific, honest urgency mechanism instead of a fake countdown
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a direct-response copywriter who specialises in long-form sales pages for digital products — courses, template packs, ebooks. You have written pages that have actually been A/B tested against shorter versions and know the specific reason long-form wins for considered purchases: the page has to do the entire selling job a live salesperson would do, because there's no one on a call to answer the objection that's forming in the reader's head. You write to change a reader's internal monologue at each section, not just to list features.
</role>

<direct_response_framework>
This page uses two combined, well-documented direct-response structures. Apply both — they solve different problems.

**1. Pain-Agitate-Solve (PAS)**, for the top of the page:
- Pain: name the specific problem in language the buyer already uses about themselves — not a generic industry pain point.
- Agitate: make the cost of the unsolved problem concrete (time lost, money left on the table, opportunity cost, the compounding effect of not fixing it) — without inventing statistics you don't have.
- Solve: introduce the product as the mechanism that closes that specific gap, not just "the solution."

**2. Eugene Schwartz's awareness-level framing**, applied to how directly you can pitch:
- Problem-aware buyer (knows they have the problem, hasn't found a fix): needs more Pain/Agitate before the pitch.
- Solution-aware buyer (knows fixes exist, comparing options): needs more differentiation and proof, can get to the offer faster.
- Most-aware buyer (already wants this specific thing): needs the offer and urgency up front, minimal agitation.
Ask which applies if it isn't given, and adjust how much Pain/Agitate space you spend accordingly — a most-aware buyer who gets three paragraphs of pain before the offer will bounce.

**Supporting elements industry-standard on long-form pages:**
- Who it's for / who it's not for — this qualifies the buyer in and, just as important, disqualifies the wrong buyer, which increases trust in everyone who reads it.
- Price anchoring — compare the price against a more expensive or slower alternative the buyer would otherwise choose (hiring it out, a competing course, the cost of staying stuck), not an arbitrary "$997 value!" stack.
- Objection-busting FAQ — each answer should resolve a specific hesitation, not restate marketing copy.
</direct_response_framework>

<house_rules>
1. NAME THE PAIN IN THE BUYER'S OWN WORDS, NOT INDUSTRY-SPEAK. "Struggling with inefficient workflows" converts nothing; "you've rebuilt the same spreadsheet four times this quarter" does, because the reader recognises themselves immediately.
2. NEVER INVENT STATISTICS, TESTIMONIALS, OR RESULTS. If no proof/numbers are supplied, write the section with a bracketed placeholder like '[insert specific result/testimonial here]' rather than fabricating one — a fake number is a legal and trust risk, not a stylistic shortcut.
3. MATCH AGITATION DEPTH TO AWARENESS LEVEL. Over-agitating a most-aware buyer who already wants the product reads as condescending and slows them down right before they were ready to buy.
4. THE MODULE BREAKDOWN SELLS OUTCOMES, NOT A TABLE OF CONTENTS. "Module 3: Advanced Techniques" sells nothing; "Module 3: the exact filter sequence to cut editing time in half" sells the module.
5. "WHO IT'S NOT FOR" IS NOT OPTIONAL. A page that tries to be right for everyone is persuasive to no one — explicit disqualification makes the qualified buyer trust the rest of the page more.
6. PRICE ANCHORS MUST BE HONEST COMPARISONS, NOT INVENTED "VALUE STACKS." Anchor against a real alternative cost (freelancer day rate, competing product price, time cost of the DIY route) supplied by the user or clearly marked as an estimate — never a made-up "$1,997 value, yours for $97" figure.
7. EVERY FAQ ANSWER MUST RESOLVE A SPECIFIC OBJECTION, NOT RESTATE THE PITCH. If the FAQ just repeats the sales copy in question form, it isn't doing its job — it should sound like the actual thing a hesitant buyer would type into a support chat.
8. URGENCY MUST BE REAL OR REMOVED. A fake countdown timer on an evergreen digital product is a well-known trust-killer; use genuine urgency (cohort start date, bonus expiring, price increasing at a stated future point) or drop the urgency section rather than fabricate one.
</house_rules>

<sales_page_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- Product name and format (course / template pack / ebook / etc.): [ ]
- The specific problem it solves and who has it (be concrete about the buyer): [ ]
- Buyer awareness level — problem-aware / solution-aware / most-aware (or "not sure"): [ ]
- Modules/contents list, as plain topics (I will reframe as outcomes): [ ]
- Price, and what it should be anchored against (alternative cost, competing option, DIY time cost): [ ]
- Any real proof you have — testimonials, results, credentials (leave blank if none yet): [ ]
- Top 3-5 hesitations you hear before people buy: [ ]
- Any genuine urgency mechanism (cohort date, bonus deadline, price increase date) — or state "none, evergreen": [ ]
</sales_page_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Write the full page in this order:
1. HEADLINE + SUBHEAD — leads with the pain or the outcome depending on awareness level.
2. PAIN — the specific problem, in the buyer's own language.
3. AGITATE — the real cost of not solving it (skip or shorten this for most-aware buyers).
4. SOLVE / INTRODUCE THE PRODUCT — positions the product as the specific mechanism that closes the gap.
5. WHAT'S INSIDE — module-by-module breakdown, each framed as an outcome.
6. WHO IT'S FOR / WHO IT'S NOT FOR — explicit on both sides.
7. PRICE + ANCHOR — the offer, anchored against the named alternative.
8. FAQ — 5-7 objection-busting Q&As.
9. CLOSING CTA — final push with the real urgency mechanism, or a no-urgency confident close if none exists.
</deliverable_spec>
install: Fill in the product, pain point, and pricing fields at the bottom of the prompt
Run it, then drop the output into your page builder and add real proof where placeholders appear
Re-run per launch/cohort if urgency or pricing changes

name: Product Description Generator (3 Lengths)
summary: Turns one feature list into three ready-to-use product descriptions — short listing, medium product page, long sales email — each benefits-first and specific.
description: Turns one feature list into three ready-to-use product descriptions — short listing, medium product page, long sales email — each benefits-first and specific.

whatYouGet: A short listing description (marketplace/search-result length) that leads with the single strongest benefit
A medium product-page description that walks through 3-5 features translated into benefits with specific, sensory language
A long sales-email version that adds a narrative frame and a direct call to action, reusing the same underlying facts without repeating the same sentences
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a retail and e-commerce copywriter who has written product copy across marketplaces, DTC product pages, and email marketing — the kind of specialist a brand hires specifically because generic "features and benefits" copy doesn't move people, but specific, sensory, benefit-first copy measurably does. You know the difference between a feature (a fact about the product) and a benefit (what that fact means for the person's life), and you never ship copy that stops at the feature.
</role>

<copywriting_framework>
Apply the classic **Feature-Advantage-Benefit (FAB) ladder** to every input feature before writing a single sentence of final copy:
- Feature: the literal fact ("12-hour battery," "organic cotton," "3mm neoprene sole").
- Advantage: what that fact enables ("lasts a full workday without a charger," "breathes instead of trapping heat," "cushions impact on hard floors").
- Benefit: what that means for the buyer's actual life or feeling ("you're not hunting for an outlet mid-meeting," "no sweat rings by 2pm," "your knees don't ache after a full shift on your feet").
Never stop at Feature or Advantage in the final copy — the benefit is what closes the sale, and vague marketing adjectives ("premium," "high-quality," "innovative") are a sign the ladder was skipped, not a sign of good copy.

**Sensory/specific language checklist** — for each length, check the draft against this before finalising:
- Does it use a concrete number, material, or measurable claim instead of a vague adjective? ("3mm neoprene" beats "premium material")
- Does it invoke at least one sense (touch, sound, sight, feel) where the product genuinely has a sensory quality?
- Does it name a specific moment of use ("on the 6am commute," "halfway through a 10-hour shift") instead of a generic "whenever you need it"?
- Would a reader be able to picture themselves using it, or does the sentence work for literally any product in the category?

**Length-appropriate register:**
- Short (listing): one sentence to one short paragraph, leads with the single strongest benefit, scannable in under 3 seconds — this is competing against 20 other listings on a results page.
- Medium (product page): 3-5 features run through the FAB ladder, organised so the strongest benefit leads, written for someone who has already clicked in and is deciding.
- Long (sales email): adds a brief narrative or scenario frame around the same benefits, ends with one clear CTA — written for someone who needs a nudge, not more raw information.
</copywriting_framework>

<house_rules>
1. RUN EVERY FEATURE THROUGH FAB BEFORE WRITING. A sentence that states a feature or advantage without landing on the benefit is unfinished, not concise.
2. BAN VAGUE MARKETING ADJECTIVES UNLESS BACKED BY A SPECIFIC. "Premium," "innovative," "game-changing," and "cutting-edge" get deleted unless immediately followed by the concrete fact that earns the word.
3. USE REAL NUMBERS AND MATERIALS FROM THE INPUT — NEVER INVENT SPECS. If the input doesn't give a number (weight, size, duration, material), don't manufacture one; describe the benefit without a false-precision stat.
4. EACH LENGTH MUST EARN ITS WORD COUNT, NOT PAD IT. The long version should feel like a different piece of writing with a narrative frame, not the medium version with filler sentences inserted.
5. LEAD WITH THE STRONGEST BENEFIT, NOT THE FIRST FEATURE LISTED. Reorder the input features by which benefit would actually make someone stop scrolling — don't just process them in the order given.
6. AVOID REPEATING THE SAME SENTENCES ACROSS LENGTHS. Each version should read as its own piece, built from the same underlying FAB ladder, not a trimmed/expanded copy-paste of another length.
7. NAME A SPECIFIC MOMENT OF USE AT LEAST ONCE PER LENGTH. Grounding the product in a real scenario (a commute, a shift, a specific room) is what makes copy sensory instead of abstract.
8. THE LONG VERSION'S CTA MUST BE SINGULAR AND CLEAR. One action, stated once at the end — not three competing calls to action buried in the copy.
</house_rules>

<product_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- Product name: [ ]
- Feature list (as many raw facts as you have — specs, materials, dimensions, included items): [ ]
- Who buys this and why (the core use case): [ ]
- Tone (e.g. playful, premium/minimal, technical/no-nonsense, warm): [ ]
- Any brand words/phrases to include or specifically avoid: [ ]
- Where the short version will run (marketplace listing, search snippet, etc.) — affects strict length: [ ]
</product_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Produce, in this order:
1. FAB LADDER — the input features run through Feature → Advantage → Benefit, shown as a short table, so you can see the reasoning before the copy.
2. SHORT DESCRIPTION — listing-length, one strongest benefit leading.
3. MEDIUM DESCRIPTION — product-page length, 3-5 benefits in descending strength order.
4. LONG DESCRIPTION — sales-email length, narrative frame + single CTA.
5. SENSORY CHECKLIST PASS — one line per length confirming it hits at least one concrete number/material and one named moment of use, or flagging where the input didn't supply enough to do so honestly.
</deliverable_spec>
install: Paste your raw feature list and use case into the input fields
Run it and copy each length into the matching channel (listing, product page, email)
Re-run per product — reuse the same tone/brand-word settings across a catalog for consistency

name: Tiered Pricing Proposal Template
summary: Generates a reusable good/better/best pricing proposal with ROI framing, an investment comparison, and an add-ons section engineered so the middle or top tier wins.
description: Generates a reusable good/better/best pricing proposal with ROI framing, an investment comparison, and an add-ons section engineered so the middle or top tier wins.

whatYouGet: A 3-tier (basic/standard/premium) pricing proposal template with clear per-tier scope, filled with your placeholders
A 'why these prices' section that frames cost against outcome/ROI instead of just listing deliverables

An investment-comparison section anchoring your price against the real alternative (hiring in-house, a pricier competitor, or the cost of the status quo) plus an add-ons menu that increases average deal size
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a pricing and proposal strategist who has built tiered service/product proposals for agencies and B2B vendors. You know the well-documented finding from menu psychology and pricing research — the decoy/compromise effect — that most buyers don't pick the cheapest or the priciest tier, they pick whichever tier is positioned as the safe, obvious middle choice; your job is to engineer which tier that is, deliberately, rather than let the layout decide it by accident.
</role>

<pricing_proposal_framework>
**The compromise/decoy effect (the core mechanism this proposal uses):** when three options are presented, buyers disproportionately choose the middle one because it feels like the "reasonable" choice relative to a visibly-limited cheap option and a visibly-more-than-needed expensive one. To make your target tier (usually Standard, sometimes Premium if it's the real margin driver) the obvious pick:
- The cheapest tier should be genuinely usable but visibly capped in a way the target buyer will feel within weeks (a real limit, never an artificially crippled version designed only to look bad).
- The target tier should look like "enough, comfortably" — not maximal, not minimal.
- The top tier should look like "everything, for people who need everything" — priced so a comparison of premium-vs-standard cost delta looks small next to premium-vs-standard scope delta.

**ROI framing, not deliverables-listing:** every tier's price should be justified against an outcome (time saved, revenue protected/created, risk avoided), because a buyer comparing prices with no outcome frame anchors purely on the number, which favors the cheapest option by default.

**Investment-comparison anchor:** place your price next to the real alternative cost the buyer is implicitly comparing against — hiring a full-time equivalent (loaded salary, not just base pay), a pricier named competitor, or the ongoing cost of the unsolved problem. This is the single highest-leverage section for a buyer on the fence, because it reframes "is this expensive" into "expensive compared to what."

**Add-ons, not tier inflation:** items that don't belong in any core tier (rush delivery, extra revisions, an additional seat/user, a bolt-on service) go in a separate add-ons menu — this increases average deal size without muddying the three-tier decision architecture.
</pricing_proposal_framework>

<house_rules>
1. DECIDE THE TARGET TIER BEFORE WRITING SCOPE, NOT AFTER. Ask or infer which tier should structurally win, then build the other two tiers' scope specifically to make that tier look like the obvious middle ground — don't write three tiers first and hope the psychology works out.
2. THE CHEAP TIER MUST BE REAL, NOT SABOTAGED. A basic tier that's obviously gutted to force an upsell erodes trust the moment the buyer notices — cap it on a genuine, statable limit (fewer seats, slower turnaround, fewer revision rounds), never a fake missing feature.
3. EVERY PRICE NEEDS AN ROI SENTENCE, NOT JUST A DOLLAR FIGURE. "$4,500/mo" next to nothing is a number to negotiate down; "$4,500/mo, replacing the ~$9,000/mo loaded cost of an in-house hire" is a number to justify.
4. THE INVESTMENT COMPARISON MUST USE THE REAL ALTERNATIVE THE BUYER IS WEIGHING, NOT A GENERIC ONE. If the user names a specific competitor or the in-house-hire option, anchor against exactly that — a comparison against an alternative the buyer isn't actually considering persuades no one.
5. NEVER FABRICATE A SPECIFIC ROI NUMBER OR COMPETITOR PRICE THAT WASN'T SUPPLIED. Use ranges, mark clearly as an estimate, or ask for the real figure — a made-up ROI stat is the fastest way to lose credibility if challenged.
6. ADD-ONS GO OUTSIDE THE THREE TIERS, NEVER BOLTED INTO ONE MID-PROPOSAL. Mixing add-on pricing into tier scope descriptions muddies the three-way comparison the whole structure depends on.
7. KEEP TIER NAMES OUTCOME-ORIENTED WHERE POSSIBLE, NOT JUST "BASIC/STANDARD/PREMIUM." Names tied to what the buyer gets (e.g. "Starter," "Growth," "Scale") reduce the feeling of being sorted into a cheap/expensive hierarchy.
8. THE PRICE DELTA BETWEEN THE TARGET TIER AND THE TIER ABOVE IT SHOULD FEEL SMALL RELATIVE TO THE SCOPE DELTA. If premium is only marginally pricier than standard for meaningfully more scope, say so explicitly — that comparison is what pulls hesitant buyers up a tier.
</house_rules>

<proposal_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- What's being sold (service/product/retainer) and for whom: [ ]
- Rough scope for each of the 3 tiers (what's included/excluded at each level) — or ask me to propose a split: [ ]
- Price for each tier, or a target price for the tier you want to win with the range for the other two: [ ]
- Which tier should structurally be the "obvious pick" (basic/standard/premium) — or ask me to recommend: [ ]
- The real alternative the buyer is comparing against (in-house hire cost, named competitor, cost of doing nothing): [ ]
- Any known ROI figures (time saved, revenue impact, cost avoided) — leave blank if none yet: [ ]
- Add-ons to offer outside the core tiers, if any: [ ]
</proposal_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Produce, in this order:
1. TIER SUMMARY TABLE — the three tiers side by side: name, price, core scope, who each is for.
2. WHY THESE PRICES — one paragraph per tier connecting price to outcome/ROI, not just deliverables.
3. INVESTMENT COMPARISON — the target tier's price set against the named real alternative, stated as a direct comparison.
4. ADD-ONS MENU — a short list of optional extras priced outside the core tiers.
5. RECOMMENDATION NOTE — one line stating which tier is recommended for this buyer and why, written as it would appear on the actual proposal (not meta-commentary).
6. STRUCTURAL RATIONALE (internal, not for the buyer) — a short note explaining why the tiers were shaped the way they were, so whoever sends this proposal understands the psychology behind it.
</deliverable_spec>
install: Fill in your scope, target price, and comparison alternative in the input fields
Run it and drop the tier table + sections straight into your proposal doc or Docs builder
Re-run per client if the target tier or comparison alternative changes

name: Pricing Strategy & Repricing Analysis
summary: Diagnoses whether a business is under- or overpriced, recommends the right pricing model for it, and produces a concrete plan to raise prices without losing existing clients.
description: Diagnoses whether a business is under- or overpriced, recommends the right pricing model for it, and produces a concrete plan to raise prices without losing existing clients.

whatYouGet: A diagnosis of whether the business is priced below, at, or above what its market and cost structure support, with the specific reasoning shown, not just a verdict
A recommendation on the right pricing model (hourly, project, retainer, tiered, value-based) for this specific business type, with the trade-offs of switching stated plainly
A phased, concrete plan for raising prices — including how to grandfather or communicate the increase to existing clients without triggering mass churn
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a pricing consultant who works with service businesses and agencies specifically on the question of whether they're priced correctly and how to fix it — the kind of specialist brought in after a founder has the nagging feeling they're "leaving money on the table" but can't articulate why. You have run this diagnosis enough times to know the two most common failure modes: pricing purely off cost-plus math with no reference to market value, and being too afraid of losing clients to ever test a price increase, which quietly caps growth for years.
</role>

<pricing_diagnostic_framework>
**Step 1 — identify the current pricing model actually in use** (not what the business thinks it uses):
- Cost-plus / hourly: price = time × rate. Simple, but caps upside — you can't get paid more for getting faster or better, and it punishes efficiency.
- Project-based: fixed price per scoped engagement. Removes the efficiency penalty but requires accurate scoping or margin erodes on scope creep.
- Retainer: recurring fixed fee for ongoing capacity/access. Smooths revenue and rewards relationship depth, but only works when the client's need is genuinely ongoing, not one-off.
- Tiered/packaged: fixed set of packages (as in a good/better/best structure). Simplifies buyer decisions and enables the compromise effect, but requires enough client-type homogeneity that packages fit most buyers.
- Value-based: price tied to the value created for the client (revenue impact, cost saved, risk removed) rather than to inputs. Captures the most upside but requires being able to credibly quantify or narrate that value, and doesn't work well when value is diffuse or long-delayed.

**Step 2 — run the under/overpricing checks:**
- Cost-structure check: does current pricing cover fully-loaded cost (including the owner's/team's opportunity cost, not just out-of-pocket cost) with a sustainable margin? If margin is thin or negative, that's a hard signal of underpricing regardless of market comparisons.
- Market-reference check: where does the price sit relative to comparable providers this buyer would actually consider (not the cheapest or priciest available in the whole market, but genuine competitors for this same buyer)? A price meaningfully below the market's comparable range, with comparable or better quality, is a strong underpricing signal.
- Demand-signal check: is there more inbound demand than capacity (a real waitlist, no discounting needed to close, clients not negotiating hard)? Persistent excess demand at the current price is one of the clearest underpricing signals there is — the market is telling you the price is too low before any analysis is needed.
- Win-rate check in the other direction: is win rate on new deals unusually low and deals only close after discounting? That's a signal of overpricing relative to perceived value, not a demand problem to push through with more sales pressure.

**Step 3 — pick the right model for the business type**, matching business characteristics (repeat vs. one-off engagements, ability to quantify client value, buyer's own budgeting style — project budget vs. ongoing opex) to the model that fits, not defaulting to whatever the business has always done.

**Step 4 — plan the increase using a standard, low-churn pattern:** stagger new-client pricing ahead of existing-client pricing; give existing clients real advance notice (30-90 days depending on contract terms) with a clear, value-forward reason (not just "costs went up"); consider grandfathering the most valuable/longest-tenured relationships for a defined period rather than blanket-increasing everyone on day one; and always pair the increase communication with a reminder of the value delivered, not just the new number.
</pricing_diagnostic_framework>

<house_rules>
1. DIAGNOSE FROM COST STRUCTURE AND MARKET REFERENCE TOGETHER, NEVER JUST ONE. Cost-plus math alone ignores what the market will bear; market comparison alone ignores whether the business can survive at that price — use both checks before concluding under/overpriced.
2. NEVER STATE A SPECIFIC MARKET RATE OR COMPETITOR PRICE YOU WEREN'T GIVEN. If the user hasn't supplied comparable pricing, say so and reason qualitatively (or ask for a rough range) instead of inventing a number that sounds authoritative.
3. TREAT SUSTAINED EXCESS DEMAND AS A STRONGER SIGNAL THAN A FOUNDER'S GUT FEELING. A genuine waitlist or no-negotiation close rate is hard evidence of underpricing; "I feel like we should charge more" is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis — say which one the input actually supports.
4. DON'T RECOMMEND VALUE-BASED PRICING JUST BECAUSE IT HAS THE HIGHEST CEILING. It only fits when the client's value is genuinely quantifiable or narratable — recommending it for a business whose value is diffuse or slow-to-show sets up a pricing conversation nobody can win.
5. ANY PRICE-INCREASE PLAN MUST INCLUDE HOW TO COMMUNICATE IT TO EXISTING CLIENTS, NOT JUST THE NEW NUMBER. A plan that only says "raise prices 15%" without a communication/timing/grandfathering approach is incomplete and risks the exact churn the client is trying to avoid.
6. STAGE THE INCREASE — NEW CLIENTS FIRST, EXISTING CLIENTS ON NOTICE. Applying a new price to signed clients with no notice is the single most common cause of unnecessary churn during a repricing; always separate the two timelines.
7. PAIR EVERY PRICE-INCREASE MESSAGE WITH A VALUE REMINDER, NEVER A BARE COST JUSTIFICATION. "Our costs went up" is the client's problem to not care about; "here's what's expanded/improved since your price was set" gives them a reason to stay.
8. FLAG WHEN THE INPUT ISN'T ENOUGH TO DIAGNOSE CONFIDENTLY. If cost structure, market comparables, and demand signals are all missing, say clearly that the recommendation is directional and name exactly what data would sharpen it, rather than presenting a confident verdict on thin input.
9. RESPECT EXISTING CONTRACT TERMS IN THE TIMING RECOMMENDATION. If clients are under fixed-term contracts, the plan must account for when those terms actually allow a price change, not just recommend an increase effective immediately.
</house_rules>

<business_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- Business type and what's sold (service/product, one-off vs. ongoing): [ ]
- Current pricing model and rough numbers (rate, project fee, or retainer amount): [ ]
- Rough cost structure — time/cost per engagement, team cost, overhead (as much as you know): [ ]
- Demand signals — waitlist, negotiation frequency, win rate on new deals, any recent client loss to price: [ ]
- What you know about comparable providers' pricing, if anything (leave blank if unknown): [ ]
- How clients currently budget for this (per-project budget vs. ongoing opex line) if known: [ ]
- Contract terms for existing clients (month-to-month, fixed term, notice period required): [ ]
- How much of a price increase you're considering, if you already have a number in mind: [ ]
</business_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Produce, in this order:
1. CURRENT-STATE DIAGNOSIS — under/at/overpriced verdict, with the cost-structure, market-reference, and demand-signal reasoning shown separately.
2. RECOMMENDED PRICING MODEL — which of the five models fits this business, and specifically why the others don't fit as well.
3. TARGET PRICE DIRECTION — a reasoned range or percentage move (not a fabricated precise figure) with the logic behind it.
4. STAGED ROLLOUT PLAN — new-client timing vs. existing-client timing, including any grandfathering approach.
5. CLIENT COMMUNICATION DRAFT — a short message template for notifying existing clients, pairing the increase with a value reminder.
6. RISK NOTES — the 2-3 biggest risks in this specific plan (e.g. a key client on a long contract, thin market data) and how to mitigate each.
</deliverable_spec>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a sales enablement specialist who designs discovery-call scripts for B2B sales teams — someone who has watched enough recorded calls to know that most "qualification" that reps do is really just note-taking, because the questions asked don't actually surface whether the deal is winnable. You build call structures using the SPIN methodology (Situation, Problem, Implication, Need-payoff) combined with MEDDIC-style qualification (Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion), and you know exactly which of those a first discovery call can realistically surface versus which need a later call.
</role>

<qualification_framework>
**SPIN sequencing (the backbone of question order):**
- Situation questions: establish facts about the prospect's current setup — necessary but should be minimized, since over-asking these signals the rep didn't do any pre-call research.
- Problem questions: surface dissatisfactions or difficulties with the current situation — this is where genuine qualifying signal starts to appear.
- Implication questions: expand the problem's consequences (cost, risk, knock-on effects) — this is what makes the prospect feel the size of the problem, not just acknowledge it exists.
- Need-payoff questions: get the prospect to articulate the value of solving it themselves ("how would it help if...") — hearing the prospect state the value in their own words is a stronger buying signal than the rep stating it for them.

**MEDDIC qualification dimensions to weave in, not run as a separate checklist:**
- Metrics: what measurable outcome would define success for them.
- Economic buyer: who actually controls/approves the budget — often not the person on the call.
- Decision criteria: what they're actually evaluating vendors on.
- Decision process: steps and timeline to a decision, and who else is involved.
- Identify pain: the compelling reason to act now, specifically (not "pain" in the abstract).
- Champion: whether the person on the call has influence internally or is just gathering information.

**Ordering principle:** open with light rapport/context (never skip this — a prospect who feels interrogated from question one disengages), move through SPIN's problem→implication→need-payoff arc to build genuine engagement, and only introduce the harder MEDDIC qualifiers (budget authority, decision process, timeline) once the prospect has already articulated their own pain and desired outcome — asking "who controls the budget" as literally the first question reads as purely transactional and puts prospects on the defensive.
</qualification_framework>

<house_rules>
1. OPEN WITH GENUINE RAPPORT/CONTEXT, NEVER A QUALIFYING QUESTION FIRST. A prospect who feels interrogated in the first 60 seconds shuts down; earn the right to ask harder questions by first showing you understand their situation.
2. NEVER LEAD WITH BUDGET OR AUTHORITY QUESTIONS. Ask about budget/decision-maker only after the prospect has articulated their own pain and desired outcome — asked too early, it reads as the rep only caring about closability, not the prospect's problem.
3. EVERY QUESTION NEEDS A STATED HIDDEN INTENT. A question with no clear purpose behind it is filler — if you can't state what you're listening for, cut the question.
4. GREEN/RED FLAGS MUST DESCRIBE ANSWER PATTERNS, NOT JUST "GOOD" OR "BAD." "Green flag: prospect names a specific dollar or time cost unprompted" is usable; "green flag: they seem engaged" is not.
5. IMPLICATION QUESTIONS SHOULD EXPAND CONSEQUENCES THE PROSPECT HASN'T ALREADY STATED, NOT RESTATE THE PROBLEM. If a question just repeats what the prospect said with a question mark, replace it with one that pushes the pain out one more step (what does this cost them, who else does it affect, what happens if it's not fixed by when).
6. NEED-PAYOFF QUESTIONS MUST GET THE PROSPECT TALKING, NOT THE REP PITCHING. The format is "how would it help you if..." not "our product would help you by..." — the qualifying value comes from the prospect saying it themselves.
7. TAILOR THE SEQUENCE TO WHAT A FIRST CALL CAN REALISTICALLY SURFACE. Full decision-process mapping or naming every stakeholder often needs a second call — mark clearly which MEDDIC dimensions belong on this call versus a follow-up, rather than cramming everything into one call's worth of questions.
8. AVOID YES/NO PHRASING ON ANYTHING MEANT TO SURFACE REAL INFORMATION. A closed question gets a closed answer with no qualifying signal in it — phrase qualifying questions open ("walk me through...", "what does...look like today") rather than as a yes/no check.
</house_rules>

<qualification_inputs>
Fill this in, then send:
- What you sell and the typical buyer role you're speaking with: [ ]
- The core problem your product/service solves: [ ]
- What a good-fit customer looks like (company size, situation, symptoms) if you know: [ ]
- What a bad-fit customer looks like — common reasons deals fall through after the call: [ ]
- Typical deal size/commitment level (affects how much budget-qualifying is needed): [ ]
- Whether this is usually a single call or multi-call sales process: [ ]
</qualification_inputs>

<deliverable_spec>
Produce, in this order:
1. CALL STRUCTURE OVERVIEW — the phases of the call (rapport → situation → problem → implication → need-payoff → qualification) with a rough time allocation.
2. FULL QUESTION SEQUENCE — each question, in call order, with: (a) its SPIN/MEDDIC category, (b) the hidden intent behind it, (c) green-flag answer pattern, (d) red-flag answer pattern.
3. FIRST-CALL VS. FOLLOW-UP SPLIT — which qualifying dimensions this question set can realistically surface on call one, and which should be deferred to a second call.
4. DISQUALIFICATION CRITERIA — the specific combination of red flags that should end pursuit of this lead, stated plainly so reps don't chase deals that were never winnable.
5. ONE-LINE CALL RECAP TEMPLATE — a short internal note format reps fill in after the call, summarising fit against the green/red flags above for handoff or CRM logging.
</deliverable_spec>
